preamble: A change from a voiced bilabial stop [b] to a voiceless velar stop [k] alters both place and voicing at once, which makes it typologically very unusual. The only well-documented case is Berawan, a group of four closely related languages in northern Sarawak, Borneo. There, pre-Berawan intervocalic *b and *g regularly surface as [k], while word-initial *b is preserved. Blust (2005) cites it as a sound change with no apparent phonetic motivation. Beguš & Dąbkowski (2023) reconstruct unattested intermediate stages (*b > *β > *ɸ > *x > k), but no Berawan dialect attests any of them, so the documented correspondence is *b > k.

examples.note: Intervocalic *b > k, while word-initial *b is retained. Beguš & Dąbkowski report that in all 36 pre-Berawan etyma with intervocalic *b or *g, the four Berawan dialects show a voiceless stop.
A further example of intervocalic *b > k from Table 1 of Beguš & Dąbkowski (data from Blust 2013 and Burkhardt 2014).

sources: Blust, R. (2005). Must sound change be linguistically motivated? Diachronica 22(2), 219–269. https://benjamins.com/catalog/dia.22.2
Beguš, G., & Dąbkowski, M. (2023). The blurring history of intervocalic devoicing. Manuscript, University of California, Berkeley. https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/007386
